# Demo Newsletter: Structuring High-Velocity Growth Experimentation

High-performing growth teams do not necessarily have better initial ideas than average teams; they have higher experimentation velocity, tighter learning loops, and disciplined prioritization.

## The ICE Prioritization Framework

When managing a growth experimentation backlog, teams should rank hypotheses using the ICE framework:
- Impact: If this experiment succeeds, how dramatically will it move our primary metric (Scale: 1 to 10)?
- Confidence: How certain are we that this will work based on qualitative feedback, past experiments, or competitor benchmarks (Scale: 1 to 10)?
- Ease: How little engineering and design effort is required to ship this test (Scale: 1 to 10)?

Prioritize tests where Ease is high and Impact is medium-to-high to maintain momentum.

## Expected Win Rates and Experimentation Discipline

In mature tech companies, only 20% to 35% of growth experiments yield statistically significant positive results. This means that 2 out of every 3 tests will fail or produce flat results. If your win rate is reported as 80%, you are almost certainly testing obvious table-stakes fixes or failing to run adequately powered A/B tests.

Key rules for experimentation rigor:
1. Never stop a test early just because it reaches significance on Day 3; run full weekly business cycles to account for day-of-week seasonality.
2. Always measure secondary guardrail metrics (e.g., ensuring an onboarding test does not harm subsequent 30-day retention or customer support ticket volume).
3. Document negative learnings rigorously so subsequent cohorts do not repeat the same flawed tests.
